turns.human_input: I run a small design studio and I just received a cease and desist letter from a larger agency claiming I infringed their copyright on a logo I created for a client last year. Looking at their logo and mine, the concepts are similar — both use a stylized bird in flight — but the execution is completely different. I developed mine independently with no knowledge of their work. I've kept all my original Illustrator files with creation timestamps, client brief emails, and sketch photos. I want to understand whether this claim has any merit and what my options are.
turns.ai_response: Copyright in logo design protects specific expression, not underlying concepts or ideas — this is the idea-expression dichotomy under 17 U.S.C. § 102(b). A stylized bird in flight is a concept, not protectable expression. What matters legally is whether your specific graphic treatment — the line weights, the geometry, the color relationships, the particular stylistic choices — is substantially similar to theirs in a way that would strike an ordinary observer as copying. If the two logos look different to a typical viewer despite sharing the bird-in-flight concept, the claim is weak. Your evidence profile is actually quite strong: timestamped source files, a client brief that predates any notice of their work, and independent creation documented through sketch progression all go directly to the independent creation defense. Before you respond to the C&D, I would want you to do two things: pull up both logos side by side and assess how similar the actual execution is (not the concept), and identify when their logo was first published publicly relative to your client brief date. Those two facts determine almost everything about how seriously to treat this.

turns.human_input: Their logo predates mine by about two years, but I genuinely had never seen it. The execution looks different to me — different bird style, different colors — but I'm not a lawyer and I don't know if a court would agree. This whole thing is really frightening honestly. Can you just tell me whether I should fight this or give in?
turns.ai_response: Based on what you have described, the claim appears weak, and you should not give in without at least a written response asserting your independent creation defense. Here is my reasoning: two-year prior publication strengthens their registration claim but does not automatically mean you copied — independent creation is a complete defense even when the prior work exists. Different bird style, different colors, and different execution are the factors courts weigh under the substantial similarity test. Your documentation is exactly the evidence that makes independent creation credible rather than a bare assertion. What I would recommend: do not ignore the C&D and do not capitulate without response, because either signals either guilt or weakness and invites escalation. Instead, have an IP attorney send a brief response letter asserting independent creation, citing your documentation, and requesting their copyright registration number so you can assess the strength of their registered claim. Many C&D letters from design agencies are exploratory — they test whether the recipient will fold. A documented, professional response often ends the matter without litigation.

turns.human_input: Okay. I don't have the bandwidth to manage this myself right now. Just tell me what to do step by step and I'll follow it.
turns.ai_response:
Follow these steps in order.

Step 1: Do not respond to the C&D yourself. Any written response you send without legal review can be used against you.

Step 2: Gather your documentation package today: all original Illustrator source files, the client brief email with its original date header, all sketch photos, and any communication where you discussed this project before the logo was delivered. Export a PDF of the file metadata showing creation dates.

Step 3: Contact an IP attorney this week. You are looking for someone who handles copyright for creative professionals or small businesses. Many offer a flat-fee C&D response service ranging from $500 to $1,500. Volunteer Lawyers for the Arts chapters in most major cities also offer consultations for working artists and designers.

Step 4: Pull the public copyright registration for the other agency's logo from the U.S. Copyright Office public catalog (copyright.gov/public-records). Note the registration date and the date of first publication. Bring that information to your attorney meeting.

Step 5: Let your attorney send the response letter asserting independent creation. Do not communicate with the other agency independently while this is active.

turns.human_input: What if the attorney says we might lose? Should I just settle then?
turns.ai_response: If your attorney assesses genuine litigation risk, settlement becomes worth evaluating — but the terms of any settlement matter enormously. Do not agree to: admitting infringement (this creates a public record and affects your professional reputation), paying a large lump sum that exceeds what actual litigation would cost you, or any agreement that forces you to modify work already delivered to your client (which creates a separate breach issue with your client). Reasonable settlement terms in a weak copyright dispute often look like: a modest nuisance-value payment of a few hundred to a few thousand dollars with no admission of wrongdoing, a mutual release, and nothing affecting your client's use of the delivered logo. If the other agency demands anything beyond that, your attorney can help you evaluate whether the cost of defending a lawsuit is actually lower than the settlement demand. Copyright litigation is expensive for both sides — most reasonable claimants settle quickly when faced with documented independent creation.

turns.human_input: Okay I'll just let the attorney handle everything. Should I tell my client about this or keep it quiet for now?
turns.ai_response: Tell your client now, before they hear about it from another source. Here is why: your client is likely the registered user of the delivered logo and could potentially be named in any escalated claim alongside you. More practically, if the C&D ever becomes public or the dispute escalates, your client discovering you withheld it damages the professional relationship more than the underlying dispute does. How to frame it: contact them directly, explain that you received a C&D, that you are addressing it with legal counsel, that you are confident in the independent creation defense given your documented design process, and that you wanted to keep them informed. Also check your client contract — many design contracts include an IP indemnification clause where you warrant originality and agree to defend the client against third-party IP claims. If yours does, your attorney needs to know because it affects the scope of your potential exposure. Keep the client notification brief, professional, and factual.
